name: diidx zah, zapoteco de San Pedro Quiatoni
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Galván Salazar, Álvaro. 2023. Esbozo fonológico del diidx zah ilustrado en textos orales de Soledad Salinas. Tesis de Maestría en Lingüística Antropológica, Escuela Nacional de Antropología e Historia, Ciudad de México (dir. Rosemary G. Beam de Azcona). 244 p. Open access, INAH repository, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Supporting: Ocotitla Maciel, Angélica Yesenia. 2025. Análisis morfosintáctico de los compuestos verbales en diidx zah. Tesis de Licenciatura en Lingüística, ENAH, Ciudad de México. 215 p.
catalog_locator: Galván 2023 p. 24 (Resumen opening ch. 3 'Estructura Segmental'); p. 77 (§4.4 Tono); also p. 17 (§2.2, bimoraic tonic rhyme), p. 80 (isolation caveat). Ocotitla Maciel 2025 §2.2.5 'Acento' pp. 24-25.
catalog_quote: [p. 24] Respecto a los tonos, el diidx zah distingue lexicamente entre un tono alto y uno bajo. El léxico es en su mayoría monosilábico por lo que dicha sílaba recibe siempre dos moras. El acento es marcado por el peso prosódico; es decir, sólo en la sílaba tónica se expresa el tipo de fonación, el tono y/o el contraste fuerte-suave. Por último, la lengua muestra un patrón acentual yámbico del tipo ligero-pesado, ahí donde se encuentran raíces bisilábicas. [p. 77] Cabe especificar que el tono, al igual que el contraste fuerte-suave y la fonación contrastiva, sólo se presenta en sílaba tónica. Las palabras morfológicamente simples en la lengua las podemos dividir en monosílabos y bisílabos. ... Por su parte, los bisílabos presentan una sílaba átona y una sílaba tónica; la sílaba átona presenta siempre una tonía media y la sílaba tónica puede presentar un tono alto o un tono bajo. [Ocotitla Maciel 2025, pp. 24-25] Asimismo, la lengua cumple con la obligatoriedad y culminatividad del acento, esto es, obligatoriamente hay uno y solo un acento primario por palabra fonológica. ... En estos casos entendemos que las palabras con más de una sílaba muestran un patrón acentual yámbico del tipo ligero-pesado. ... Observaremos que el requisito de bimoraicidad se sigue en la última sílaba de los compuestos, contando con su acento como palabras fonológicas.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: [p. 24] The lexicon is mostly monosyllabic, so that syllable always receives two moras. Stress is marked by prosodic weight; that is, only in the stressed syllable are phonation type, tone and/or the fortis–lenis contrast expressed. Finally, the language shows an iambic light–heavy stress pattern wherever bisyllabic roots are found. [p. 77] Bisyllables, for their part, have an unstressed syllable and a stressed syllable; the unstressed syllable always has mid pitch and the stressed syllable may carry a high or a low tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Roots are overwhelmingly monosyllabic and that syllable is stressed (obligatorily bimoraic; it is the only syllable that carries tone, phonation type and the fortis–lenis contrast). When a word has more than one syllable (bisyllabic roots, aspect prefix + root such as ka-jáʔp 'está subiendo', and compounds) stress is iambic, light–heavy, i.e. on the final heavy syllable; Ocotitla Maciel 2025 (p. 24-27, citing Galván) adds that stress is obligatory and culminative (exactly one primary stress per phonological word) and that in compounds the bimoraic, stressed syllable is the last one. The 'final' syllable is the root syllable; person enclitics (=a 1s, =ge 3s) attach after the root and are toneless, so within the stem stress is root-final. Tone (H vs L) is contrastive only on the stressed syllable — a tonal language with word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Ocotitla Maciel 2025 (p. 24) states there is one and only one primary stress per phonological word (culminativity); no secondary stress is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Galván p. 80: the tonal statements hold for words elicited in isolation; in connected texts tone often changes or disappears when two tonic syllables are adjacent, and whether one tonic syllable takes priority is left open. Text notes (p. 107, 116) record occasional higher pitch on a post-tonic syllable. Loanwords not discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root with prefixes/compounds), words elicited in isolation; author is explicit that the description is of the variety of La Soledad Salinas (southern part of the municipality of San Pedro Quiatoni) and notes minor segmental variation among the municipality's localities.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement comes from Galván Salazar 2023, which describes the diidx zah of La Soledad Salinas, a community at the southern edge of the municipality of San Pedro Quiatoni (Tlacolula district, Oaxaca); the author notes small segmental differences among the municipality's localities (San Pablo Lachiriega, La Soledad Salinas, San Pedro Quiatoni cabecera, La Mancornada, Unión Juárez, El Porvenir per Ocotitla Maciel 2025 p. 7). Glottolog has no separate dialect code for Soledad Salinas; all of this falls under sanp1261 / ISO zpf. Vázquez Beltrán 2023 and Ocotitla Maciel 2025 draw on speakers from San Pablo Lachiriega and Soledad Salinas as well as the cabecera.

sources.note: §2.2.5 'Acento', p. 24 (p. 35), restating Galván 2023: the tonic syllable always gets two moras and is where phonation, tone and fortis-lenis contrast; stress is obligatory and culminative — exactly one primary stress per phonological word; polysyllabic words (aspect prefix + root, e.g. ka-jáʔp 'está subiendo', and compounds) show an iambic light-heavy pattern; in compounds the bimoraicity requirement falls on the last syllable and a single stress with iambic rhythm is observed (pp. 24-27).

sources.citation: Vázquez Beltrán, Virginia. 2023. Clases verbales en diidx zah, zapoteco de Quiatoni. Tesis de Licenciatura en Lingüística, ENAH, Ciudad de México (dir. Rosemary G. Beam de Azcona; asesor Hiroto Uchihara). 166 p.
sources.note: Ch. 2 (pp. 32-46) is a phonology sketch that explicitly defers to Galván Salazar for detail. Says only that in stressed syllables vowels are phonetically long before lenis consonants or in open syllables and short before fortis consonants (p. 41); discusses historical loss of pretonic (prefix) and post-tonic vowels; no synchronic stress-placement rule stated.
